help.intro: A small group of very common verbs change their stem vowel in the present tense — but only in two forms, du and er/sie/es. Everything else about them is regular: the endings are the usual -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en, and ich, wir, ihr and sie/Sie keep the vowel of the infinitive. There are three kinds of change — a becomes ä (fahren → du fährst), e becomes i (sprechen → du sprichst, essen → du isst) and e becomes ie (lesen → du liest, sehen → du siehst). The eight verbs in this quiz are among the most common in everyday German and cover most of what you will meet; nehmen is the odd one out, doubling the m and losing the h: du nimmst, er nimmt. Because the umlaut is the whole point here, it is checked strictly: fahrst for fährst is marked wrong (type ae if your keyboard has no ä).
help.tips[0].title: Only du and er/sie/es change
help.tips[0].text: ich fahre — du fährst — er fährt — wir fahren — ihr fahrt — sie fahren. The change lives in the middle two forms and nowhere else.
help.tips[0].examples[0].en: I sleep late. You sleep late. He sleeps late.
help.tips[0].examples[1].en: We sleep, you sleep, they sleep — no change.
help.tips[0].check.why: Only du and er/sie/es get the umlaut. wir keeps the infinitive vowel: wir fahren.
help.tips[1].title: a → ä, e → i, e → ie
help.tips[1].text: fahren/schlafen take the umlaut. sprechen/essen/nehmen/geben go to i. lesen/sehen go to ie. Learn each verb with its du-form: fahren–fährst, lesen–liest, essen–isst.
help.tips[1].examples[0].en: You read a book. He watches a film.
help.tips[1].examples[1].en: You speak German well. She eats an apple.
help.tips[1].check.why: sprechen is an e → i verb: er/sie spricht.
help.tips[2].title: nehmen and essen shrink
help.tips[2].text: nehmen: du nimmst, er nimmt (double m, no h). essen: du isst, er isst — the -st merges with the stem's ss. lesen also: du liest, not 'liesst'.
help.tips[2].examples[0].en: I take the bus. He takes the car.
help.tips[2].examples[1].en: What are you eating? – I'm eating bread.
help.tips[2].check.why: nehmen loses the h and doubles the m: du nimmst.
help.tips[3].title: The endings are still regular
help.tips[3].text: The vowel changes; the ending does not. du = -st, er = -t. So du fährst (not du fähr), er gibt (not er gib).
help.tips[3].examples[0].en: You give me the book. He gives it to you.
help.tips[3].examples[1].en: You are going to Berlin. He is going to Vienna.
help.tips[3].check.why: The vowel changes to ä, but the er-ending -t stays: er fährt.
help.remember[0]: 'du and er change, the rest stay square' — say a verb's du-form aloud each time you learn it.
help.remember[1]: If you hear an umlaut or an i in a verb, look for du or er in front of it.
help.context.en: In the morning Lisa takes the bus to work. She reads the paper and eats a roll. Her colleague talks a lot and always has a coffee. And you? Do you take the bus too? What do you like reading?
help.mistakes[0].why: Only du and er/sie/es change; wir, ihr and sie keep the infinitive vowel.
help.mistakes[1].why: These verbs must change in du and er — the unchanged form is the error.
help.hook: A handful of everyday verbs change their vowel for just two people — du and er/sie/es — and stay normal everywhere else.
sentences[0].english: Do you take the bus to work?
sentences[0].why: fahren changes a → ä in the du and er/sie/es forms only: du fährst.
sentences[1].english: My father is going to Berlin on Monday.
sentences[1].why: mein Vater = er, and er/sie/es gets the vowel change a → ä: fährt.
sentences[2].english: Do you sleep in on Sunday?
sentences[2].why: schlafen changes a → ä for du: schläfst.
sentences[3].why: das Baby = es, and er/sie/es takes the a → ä change: schläft.
sentences[4].why: lesen changes e → ie for du, and the stem's s merges with -st: du liest.
sentences[5].why: Lisa = sie, and er/sie/es takes e → ie: liest — the same form as du here.
sentences[6].english: Do you see the car over there?
sentences[6].why: sehen changes e → ie for du: siehst.
sentences[7].english: He watches a film in the evening.
sentences[7].why: er/sie/es takes the e → ie change: sieht.
sentences[8].why: sprechen changes e → i (short) for du: sprichst.
sentences[9].why: mein Kollege = er, and er/sie/es takes e → i: spricht.
sentences[10].english: What do you eat for breakfast?
sentences[10].why: essen changes e → i for du, and its ss merges with -st: du isst.
sentences[11].why: er/sie/es takes e → i: isst — spelt the same as the du form.
sentences[12].english: Are you taking the bus or the car?
sentences[12].why: nehmen changes e → i and doubles the m for du: nimmst — the h disappears too.
sentences[13].why: er/sie/es of nehmen is nimmt — e → i, double m, no h.
sentences[14].english: What are you giving Anna for her birthday?
sentences[14].why: geben changes e → i for du: gibst.
sentences[15].english: The teacher gives a lot of homework.
sentences[15].why: der Lehrer = er, and er/sie/es takes e → i: gibt.
sentences[16].english: We sleep in at the weekend.
sentences[16].why: The vowel change touches only du and er/sie/es — wir keeps the plain stem: schlafen.
sentences[17].why: ihr never takes the vowel change: esst, with the plain e.
sentences[18].english: I read the newspaper every day.
sentences[18].why: ich never takes the vowel change: lese, with the plain e.
sentences[19].english: My parents are going to Italy.
sentences[19].why: Plural sie keeps the plain stem — no umlaut: fahren.
sentences[20].english: Are you talking to him this evening?
sentences[20].why: sprechen takes e → i for du: Sprichst.
sentences[21].why: Oma = sie, and er/sie/es of geben is gibt — e → i.
